edges.description: Reduced receptor activation lowers signaling through the downstream kinase cascades.
Hypothalamic TrkB signaling suppresses food intake in mice; in patients the affected neurons have not been identified, so this link is inferred from model organisms.
edges.target: Loss of TrkB-Mediated Hypothalamic Satiety Signaling

edges.description: Reduced TrkB signaling diminishes BDNF-driven neurite growth and synapse formation.
The index patient had reduced nociception, which the authors attribute to the role of TrkB in the nervous system; the pathway involved is not characterized.
Removal of a hypothalamic anorexigenic signal increases food intake.
edges.source: Loss of TrkB-Mediated Hypothalamic Satiety Signaling

edges.description: Defective neurite growth and synapse formation are proposed to underlie the neurodevelopmental phenotype; this has not been tested in patient neurons.
Impaired hippocampal synaptogenesis is proposed to contribute to the learning and memory deficits.
Sustained excess food intake produces early-onset obesity.
Reduced TrkB dosage in the mouse reproduces the hyperphagic weight gain of the human disease.
edges.limitations: TrkB is reduced throughout the body rather than by a heterozygous patient allele, and the weight gain was reported on higher-fat diets. The model does not address the neurodevelopmental features.
edges.target: Loss of TrkB-Mediated Hypothalamic Satiety Signaling

edges.description: Removing TrkB from one hypothalamic nucleus is sufficient for hyperphagic obesity.
edges.limitations: The deletion is complete and regionally restricted, whereas patients are heterozygous throughout the body, and it says nothing about the neurodevelopmental features.

nodes.description: BDNF binding fails to activate the TrkB effector pathways normally, with reduced MAP kinase, phospholipase C-gamma and Akt activation in cells expressing the p.Tyr722Cys receptor.

evidence.reference_title: Functional characterization of human NTRK2 mutations identified in patients with severe early-onset obesity.
evidence.snippet: Further functional characterization of the previously reported Y722C TrkB mutation reveals impaired activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase, phospholipase C-gamma and Akt, as well as reduced BDNF-induced neurite outgrowth and cell survival in stably transfected PC12 cell lines.

nodes.description: Patient TrkB variants reduce BDNF-induced neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival, and some act dominantly to inhibit glutamatergic synapse formation in hippocampal neurons. This is the proposed basis of the developmental delay and the learning and memory deficits.

evidence.reference_title: Human BDNF/TrkB variants impair hippocampal synaptogenesis and associate with neurobehavioural abnormalities.
evidence.snippet: Multiple variants in the kinase domain and one variant in the extracellular domain of TrkB led to a loss of function through multiple signalling pathways, impaired neurite outgrowth and dominantly inhibited glutamatergic synaptogenesis in hippocampal neurons.

nodes.description: Reduced nociception, reported in the index patient.

evidence.reference_title: A de novo mutation affecting human TrkB associated with severe obesity and developmental delay.
evidence.snippet: The associated impairment in memory, learning and nociception seen in the proband reflects the crucial role of TrkB in the human nervous system.

nodes.description: TrkB-expressing neurons of the paraventricular and dorsomedial hypothalamus suppress food intake, and BDNF acts as an effector of melanocortin-4 receptor signaling in the ventromedial hypothalamus. Loss of TrkB signaling in these circuits removes an anorexigenic signal. This node is established in mice; it is inferred, not demonstrated, in patients.

nodes.description: Truncating NTRK2 variants, and missense variants that are predicted to disrupt the folded structure of TrkB or that fall in the kinase domain, reduce BDNF-stimulated TrkB activity. The index p.Tyr722Cys variant impairs receptor autophosphorylation. Several kinase-domain variants act dominantly in neurons, so reduced signaling may reflect dominant-negative interference as well as haploinsufficiency.
